tracks.title: Pausing a computer is supposed to be hard
tracks.text: Lesson two point three — sandboxes. A sub-lesson, under the Nexus… and it opens with a claim the whole industry would dispute. Suspension is a file operation. Here is the problem it answers. Pausing a computer is supposed to be hard. Everyone selling agent infrastructure sells the same expensive miracle — we can freeze your micro V M. Snapshot the guest memory… track the dirty pages… ship gigabytes to object storage… meter the hibernation… and charge for the thaw. The pitch works because the assumption underneath it feels like physics. If an agent works on a rented virtual machine, then pausing it really is heavyweight, resuming it really is slow, and somebody really does have to bill you for both. [curious] But the Nexus lesson already dismantled the twin of that assumption — isolation there is construction, not a rented perimeter. This page runs the identical move on state. If the thing you are pausing is not a machine… if its entire durable state is one file, and the process holding it is disposable by contract… then suspension stops being a systems feat. It becomes what it always should have been. A filing decision.

tracks.title: The five states
tracks.text: First — the definition. A sandbox is the running shape of a docked workbook. One WebAssembly instance, under one supervised process, whose entire durable state is one SQLite file… and whose whole life is five explicit states. Created… active… suspended… frozen… archived. Plus deleted — the only exit. Two facts before the map. First, the state lives in a registry row, not in the process. A sandbox can be deep in cold storage and still be a first-class citizen of the system, because being a citizen costs one row. Second, transitions are explicit. The engine validates every hop against a map and answers either ok… or error, invalid. No implicit shortcuts. And the entire map is six lines of code — short enough to read aloud. Created may become active. Active may become suspended, or be archived. Suspended may return to active, or go on to frozen. Frozen may return to active, or be archived. And archived may be revived back to active… or deleted. That is the lifecycle product, in full. [curious] Now — two edges in that map are the ones people get wrong, and both are deliberate. First, an active sandbox cannot freeze directly. There is no active-to-frozen hop. Freezing is earned by neglect, not commanded — a sandbox idles into suspended first, and only a suspended sandbox can go cold. Second, a frozen sandbox thaws straight back to active. No re-warming ladder… no passing back through suspended. Going cold is gradual. Coming back is one step. Even archived is revivable — archived to active is in the map. The only state you cannot leave… is deleted.

tracks.title: Warm and cold
tracks.text: Next — warm and cold… the only distinction that actually matters. Underneath the five names there is really just one. A session is warm when its Instance is live in the BEAM — and checking costs a single registry lookup. It is cold when only its V F S file persists. Every state below active is just cold… filed in a different drawer. Walk the drawers with me. Active — a live, supervised process, with its file open in the live directory. Suspended — the process is gone, but the file is still local. That local file is the warm cache, so resume is immediate. Frozen — the process is gone, and the file has been copied out to cold storage… so resume costs one copy back. Created and archived — registry rows pointing at a drawer, waiting. One resume function reconciles all of it. Call resume on a warm session, and the answer is warm, already active — the running Instance is reused and nothing is touched. Call it on a cold one, and the cold path runs — resolve the file, start the Instance under the supervisor, flip the registry row to active. And here is the whole machine in one real demo, end to end. Register a session — sess eight forty one, tenant acme. The registry writes one row… state, created. Resume it once — the cold path runs, and the call returns cold. Resume it a second time — warm, already active. [chuckles] Ask the registry, and the row says active. That is the entire lifecycle, exercised in four calls. One more verb worth knowing — prefetch. Prefetch-on-auth pulls a session file local, restoring from cold storage if needed, without starting the Instance. The login warms the cache… so the first real request lands on a local file instead of a cold fetch.

tracks.title: Stop the process, keep the file
tracks.text: Now the trick itself. Stop the process… keep the file. Elsewhere, freezing a sandbox is a memory-snapshot A P I call you pay for — guest RAM serialized, device state captured, restore measured in seconds and cents. Here is the shipped implementation of freeze, and I can read it aloud in one breath. Make the cold directory if it does not exist. Copy the V F S file into it, named by session. Return the frozen path. [exhales] That is the entire function. The engine documentation states the philosophy outright — the SQLite file is the durable state. Freeze is stop the process, keep the file… no V M snapshot. Resume is the same trick reversed, plus one act of hygiene. Picture the sequence. Going down — the host terminates the Instance, because the process is disposable… then copies the live file into cold storage. That copy is the entire snapshot. Coming back — the host copies the file from cold storage to the live directory… clears the t m p volume, where scratch dies… and starts a fresh Instance, flipping the registry row to active. [curious] The obvious objection — what about everything in memory? The answer is the contract that makes this whole page possible. Components here are stateless between calls — re-instantiated at every Instance start — so there is no precious linear memory to capture. A component that wants durable state declares persist… which is a promise to checkpoint that state into the V F S, where the runtime actually guarantees durability. The engine even walks the recursive plan — nested sub-workflows included — and returns exactly the components that opted in. In the engine's own words… the V F S is the orthogonal persistence layer. A raw memory snapshot is not missing. It does not fit a stateless component, and it is not exposed. A non-goal — not a gap.

tracks.title: The demotion ladder
tracks.text: Next — the demotion ladder. Who decides when a sandbox goes cold? Policy… written as two constants and one pure function. Picture a slide running left to right. On the left, active — lit up green, because someone, or some schedule, is here. Fifteen idle minutes… and it slides to suspended. Process gone, file still local. Twenty-four idle hours after that… and it slides to frozen. File copied to cold storage. And then only a dotted line continues to archived — because frozen never auto-archives. Archiving is a decision, not a decay. The constants are exactly what I said — fifteen minutes to suspend, twenty-four hours to freeze — and the demo proves the function in four answers. Active and sixteen minutes idle… suspended. Active and fresh… nil, stay put. Suspended and two days idle… frozen. Frozen, no matter how long… stays frozen. [excited] What the ladder buys is the economics of the whole model. A thousand docked workbooks can exist while only a handful are warm, because an idle sandbox costs a registry row and a file… not a running V M. And note what counts as activity — a request landing, a schedule firing, an agent doing its rounds. Anything that touches the sandbox resets its idle clock. One honest precision before we move on. That function is pure policy. The thresholds are shipped, real, and demo-proven… but the driver that applies them on a tick is the session registry's job. So do not hear this as a promise that a ticker is demoting your sessions tonight. The honest framing — demotion is what the system is built to do… at exactly these thresholds.

tracks.title: One table runs the building
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — one table runs the building. Skippable on the page… worth a minute here. Something has to remember ten thousand sandboxes while most of them are cold. The engine's answer comes from the control plane's first line of documentation. SQLite is the control plane… the data plane is each Instance's own V F S. Postgres is only needed if we go multi-machine. The whole bureaucracy is one table, with five columns. First — i d, the session. Second — tenant, whose it is. Third — state… created, active, suspended, frozen, or archived. Fourth — the V F S path, where the disk lives. And fifth — updated, an epoch timestamp the idle clock reads. One example row reads… sess eight forty one — acme — active — a live path — and a timestamp. That row is the entire lifecycle bureaucracy for one sandbox. Register inserts it at created… set-state flips it and stamps the clock… and the control plane serves the whole list over H T T P as JSON. A second table stores each workbook's org source — the deployable artifact itself. Two honest notes. The registry's database path comes from one environment variable, W B underscore REGISTRY… and it defaults to in-memory. Out of the box, the bookkeeping itself is volatile — a durable registry is one env var away, but it is your env var. And this is the single-machine story by design. Multi-machine swaps the SQLite registry for Postgres — the same flow… a different registry.

tracks.title: What survives the winter
tracks.text: Next — what survives the winter. The file being frozen is the V F S — one SQLite store with three named volumes, and each volume has its own survival contract. First, workspace — the working tree, the work itself. It survives freeze and resume… and it is the one volume that ships when you share. Second, memory — the agent's long-term memory, what it learned. It survives freeze and resume… but it is stripped on egress. Third, t m p — scratch. It never ships… and resume clears it, by name, every time. The proof is a round trip you can run. The demo writes the same path into all three volumes — the workbook files into workspace… what the agent learned into memory… and the word scratch into t m p. Then it freezes, resumes, and reads back. Workspace — ok, the workbook files. Memory — ok, what the agent learned. T m p — error. [chuckles] T m p dying is not a bug. Resume literally clears the t m p volume on restore… because scratch that survived hibernation would not be scratch. And notice the asymmetry hiding in that contract — freeze keeps more than sharing does. Cold storage is yours, so the agent's memory rides along. Egress is for others, so only the workspace ships — the public volumes list is exactly one entry long. Freezing and sharing both move the same file, with different strip rules… because they answer to different audiences.

tracks.title: One template, many tenants
tracks.text: Another depth rung — one template, many tenants. Once state-is-a-file has paid for freeze… it keeps paying. Multi-tenant provisioning — elsewhere a golden-image pipeline — is the same file copy, pointed forwards. Picture the diagram. At the top, one box — base dot sqlite, the seeded template. Read-only… never mutated. Two arrows fall from it, each labeled file copy. One lands on a fresh file for tenant acme… the other on a fresh file for tenant globex. The demo runs exactly that, and the checks come back exactly as isolation demands. Both tenants inherit the seed. Neither sees the other's writes. And the base is untouched. [curious] So hold the two tricks side by side. Freeze is a copy pointed backwards — current state into cold storage. Clone is a copy pointed forwards — a template into a tenant's future. One primitive… both directions.

tracks.title: Two clocks of durability
tracks.text: The last depth rung — two clocks of durability. Because freeze is a filing decision, not a backup. It captures the file at a lifecycle moment… and between moments, a crash would still cost you the gap. So durability runs on two clocks at once, over the same file. First — freeze. Point-in-time… a lifecycle event copies the file to cold storage. Second — litestream. Continuous… write-ahead-log changes stream to a replica as they happen, completely independent of lifecycle state. A suspended sandbox's last writes are as replicated as an active one's. Mechanically — the database runs in W A L mode, which is one pragma… and an external litestream binary holds a long-lived port per replicated database, streaming changes out of band. The engine never blocks on it. And the replica address is the only thing that changes between development and production. A file U R L locally… an S three bucket in production. Same command — only the U R L and the credentials differ. Restore is a single one-shot command, replica back to a fresh file — the disaster path is one verb. Two clocks… one file… and neither mechanism needed to know about the other. Freeze decides where the file is filed. Litestream makes sure it cannot be lost.

tracks.title: What this isn't
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what this is not. Four limits, stated plainly. First — there is no linear-memory snapshot, and not as a missing feature. A component that keeps state in WebAssembly memory and never declares persist… loses that state at suspend. That is the contract — durable state belongs in the V F S, and the system is honest enough to make the alternative impossible, rather than unreliable. Second — the idle tick is policy-complete, driver-pending. The thresholds are shipped constants and the function is demo-proven… but applying them on a schedule is the session registry's job. Third — the registry defaults to memory. Leave that environment variable unset, and the control plane's own bookkeeping is volatile. [sighs] One env var… but yours to set. Fourth — this is the single-machine flow. Multi-machine swaps SQLite for Postgres, same flow, different registry… and that story is not this page. Two smaller candors to close. Archived has a place in the map and the registry, and no dedicated machinery beyond them — no archive helper exists yet. And none of this applies to an undocked workbook file at all. A file sitting in your repo has no lifecycle to manage… because there is no process to stop. The state machine begins at docking.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] If I close my laptop, is my agent's work gone? Your laptop was never the question — a docked sandbox lives on the engine. The worst case is demotion down the ladder… suspended, then frozen. Both are just the file in a different drawer, and resume brings it straight back. What is actually different between suspended and frozen? In both, the process is gone and only the file remains. Suspended keeps it in the live directory — the warm cache. Frozen has copied it to cold storage. That copy is the entire mechanical difference the code shows. Does resume lose anything? Exactly one thing, on purpose — the t m p volume, cleared by name on every restore. Workspace and memory survive… the demo proves the round trip. Is freeze a backup? No. Freeze is a filing decision — a point-in-time copy at a lifecycle moment. The backup is litestream… continuous, lifecycle-independent, restorable in one command. Can an archived sandbox come back? Yes — archived to active is in the map. Archive is a long-term drawer, not a grave… and nothing in the map or the idle policy ever deletes on its own. And — why can I not freeze an active sandbox directly? [chuckles] Because the map says no. Freezing is earned by neglect — fifteen idle minutes to suspend, twenty-four suspended hours to freeze. The thaw, though… is one step.

tracks.title: Back up to the Nexus
tracks.text: So that is the sandbox lifecycle. Five states… a six-line map… and the heaviest operation in the whole machine is a file copy — because the durable state was always one file, and the process was always disposable. [curious] The way back up is short. This page stands under the Nexus — lesson two — the engine that is isolated, stateful, and agentic. The Nexus made that three-part promise… and this lesson was the stateful word, run through time. From there, the siblings. Capabilities — what an active sandbox may reach while it runs. And the V F S — lesson nine — the disk itself… the very file this whole page has been copying. If suspension as a filing decision made sense to you… you already understand the Nexus better than most of the industry understands its hypervisor bill.
